subject: science
passage: For much of the twentieth century, many people believed that dogs see the world only in shades of black, white, and gray. Because dogs rely so heavily on their sense of smell, it seemed reasonable to assume that color vision would be of little use to them.
passage_b: The retina contains cone cells, which allow animals to detect color. Humans typically have three types of cones, while dogs have two. Studies in which dogs were trained to choose between colored panels show that they can tell blue from yellow but have trouble telling red from green. Their color vision, in other words, resembles that of a person with red-green color blindness.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that dogs are unable to distinguish any colors at all
choices.B: By noting that dogs see some colors, though fewer than most people
choices.C: By suggesting that dogs actually depend more on sight than on smell
choices.D: By arguing that dogs see colors just as well as most humans can

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the belief that dogs see "only in shades of black, white, and gray." Text 2 says dogs have two types of cones and "can tell blue from yellow" but struggle with red and green. So the author of Text 2 would say dogs do see color, but a narrower range than most humans.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says dogs can tell blue from yellow, so they can distinguish some colors.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 explains that dogs distinguish blue from yellow but not red from green, so they see some colors but fewer than most people.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 does not compare how much dogs rely on sight and on smell.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says dogs have fewer cone types than humans and have trouble with red and green.
